paragraphs.text: The desert locust is perhaps the most destructive migratory pest in the world. For most of the time, it lives a quiet, solitary life in the deserts of North Africa, the Middle East and South-West Asia, an area covering some sixteen million square kilometres. Solitary locusts are green or brown, avoid one another and fly mainly at night. Under certain conditions, however, they undergo a remarkable transformation.

When unusually heavy rains fall in the desert, vegetation grows rapidly and locusts breed in large numbers. As the plants dry out again, the insects are forced together in the remaining patches of green. Experiments have shown that the repeated touching of the hind legs, caused by crowding, triggers a release of the chemical serotonin in the locust's nervous system. Within a few hours, the insects begin to seek each other out rather than avoid each other. Over the following generations, they change colour to yellow and black, develop larger muscles and become active during the day. This is known as the gregarious phase.

Gregarious locusts form bands of wingless young insects, called hoppers, which march across the ground, and later swarms of flying adults. A single swarm can cover several hundred square kilometres and contain tens of billions of insects. Each adult can eat roughly its own weight in fresh food, about two grams, every day, which means that a swarm of one square kilometre can consume as much food in a day as 35,000 people. Carried by the wind, swarms can travel up to 150 kilometres in a day.

Major outbreaks, known as plagues, have been recorded since ancient times. The most recent serious plague, between 1987 and 1989, affected more than forty countries. In 2019 and 2020, after cyclones brought heavy rain to the Arabian Peninsula, swarms spread across East Africa and South Asia. Kenya experienced its worst invasion for seventy years, and the United Nations warned that the food security of millions of people was at risk.

Control of locusts has relied mainly on chemical pesticides sprayed from vehicles or aircraft. These are effective but can harm other insects, birds and people, and they are expensive to apply over large areas. A biological alternative, based on a fungus that infects and kills locusts but is harmless to most other animals, has been available since the late 1990s. It acts more slowly than chemical pesticides, taking up to two weeks to kill the insects, which has limited its use during emergencies.

Most experts agree that the most effective strategy is prevention. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations runs a monitoring system that combines satellite data on rainfall and vegetation with reports from field teams in affected countries. When conditions favour breeding, teams can treat small groups of locusts before they become swarms. This approach is far cheaper than fighting a plague: the response to the 2003-2005 outbreak in West Africa cost an estimated 570 million dollars, whereas the annual cost of prevention is a small fraction of that.
